items.prompt: Which of these is a germ that can cause disease?
hints: It is a tiny living thing.
items.explanation: Bacteria are tiny living things and some cause disease.

items.prompt: Which of these helps keep food safe to eat?

options.why: Warm food lets germs grow fast.

items.explanation: Clean hands help stop germs reaching food.

items.prompt: Skin is a ___ that helps keep germs out of the body.
hints: It covers the outside of the body.
items.explanation: Skin is a barrier against germs.

items.prompt: How can water spread disease?

options.text: Dirty water can carry germs that make people ill.
Only salty water can carry germs.
options.why: Fresh water can carry germs too.

items.explanation: Dirty water can hold germs, so drinking it can cause diseases.

items.prompt: Why do we boil drinking water in some places?

options.text: to kill germs in the water

items.explanation: Boiling kills many germs, so the water is safer to drink.

items.prompt: Which part of the body makes acid that kills many germs?
hints: It is where food goes after you swallow.
The acid breaks down food too.
items.explanation: The stomach makes acid that kills many germs that arrive with food.

items.prompt: What do tiny hairs and mucus in the nose do?

options.text: They catch dirt and germs before they reach the lungs.
They make you sneeze for fun.

hints: The nose is a doorway for air.
Germs can come in with the air.
items.explanation: Hairs and mucus trap dirt and germs, which helps protect the lungs.

items.prompt: Sort each action into helping to stop the spread of disease or helping it to spread.

items.text: covering your cough with a tissue

hints: Sharing and dirty water spread them.
items.explanation: Hygiene stops germs spreading. Sharing personal items or drinking dirty water can spread them.

items.prompt: Which of these are ways germs can spread?

options.why: Germs do not pass by looking.
Talking does not spread germs unless droplets travel.

hints: Water and air can carry them.
items.explanation: Germs can spread through dirty water and through droplets in the air.

items.prompt: What do white blood cells do?

options.text: They carry oxygen to the cells.
They fight germs that get inside the body.

hints: They are part of the blood.
items.explanation: White blood cells find and fight germs inside the body.

items.prompt: A cut in the skin lets germs into the body. Why is it important to wash and cover it?

options.text: to keep germs out while the skin heals

hints: A cover acts like skin for a while.
items.explanation: Cleaning and covering a cut protects it from germs while the skin heals.

items.prompt: Which of these is a way to stop the spread of germs when you sneeze?

options.text: sneeze into a tissue or your elbow

items.explanation: Sneezing into a tissue or elbow catches the droplets.

items.prompt: Why do doctors recommend vaccines?

options.text: They help the body get ready to fight certain germs before you meet them.
They kill all germs in the world.
options.why: They only help your own body.

hints: A vaccine is given in advance.
items.explanation: A vaccine trains the body to respond to a germ, so it can fight it quickly.

items.prompt: Tiny things that can cause disease are called ___ or microbes.
hints: They are too small to see.
items.explanation: Germs, or microbes, can cause infectious diseases.

items.prompt: Why can a disease spread quickly in a school?

options.text: Many people are close together, so germs pass easily.

hints: Think about how close children sit.
Germs spread by touch and air.
items.explanation: When people are close, germs have more chances to pass between them.

items.prompt: A child is ill with a fever. Which action is the best?

options.text: rest, drink water and tell an adult

hints: Rest helps the body fight germs.
Fever is a sign of infection.
items.explanation: Resting, drinking water and telling an adult is the best way to get better and protect others.

items.prompt: Why does washing hands before eating help?

options.text: It makes the food taste sweeter.
It removes germs that could get into the body with food.
It makes the stomach acid stronger.
options.why: Washing hands does not change the stomach.

hints: Eating moves germs into the body.
items.explanation: Clean hands carry fewer germs into the mouth when you eat.

items.prompt: Why can antibiotics not cure a cold?

options.text: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work on bacteria.
Colds are not caused by anything.

hints: There are different kinds of germs.
A cold is caused by a virus.
items.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses, which cause colds.

items.prompt: A town has no clean drinking water and many people become ill. Which is the most useful change?

options.text: provide clean water and good sanitation

options.why: This does not fix the cause.

items.explanation: Clean water and sanitation remove the main route for germs, so fewer people become ill.

items.prompt: Which sentence about vaccines is correct?

options.text: A vaccine is the same as a medicine for an illness you already have.
A vaccine helps the body to be ready for a germ before it arrives.
A vaccine makes you ill on purpose.
options.why: A vaccine is designed to be safe.

hints: They are different from medicine for an illness you already have.
items.explanation: A vaccine prepares the immune system in advance so it can respond quickly.

items.prompt: True or false: Bacteria and viruses are two kinds of germs.
items.explanation: Both can cause diseases, and they are too small to see.

items.prompt: True or false: Skin is no help in defending the body from germs.
hints: Does a cut let germs in?
items.explanation: Skin is a barrier that keeps germs out. Mucus in the nose and acid in the stomach also help.

items.prompt: True or false: White blood cells help the body to fight germs that get inside.
items.explanation: They find and destroy germs, or make substances that do so.

items.prompt: True or false: Illnesses spread only by touching a sick person.
items.explanation: They can also spread through the air in droplets, on dirty surfaces, in food and water, and by animals.
